# Exercise 5.3 — Decision trees, overfitting and tuning {#sec-decision-trees}

A decision tree predicts by asking yes-or-no questions: is glucose above 128?
If so, is body mass above 30? Each answer sends a person down one branch until
they reach a **leaf**, which gives a predicted class and a probability. Trees
are easy to read. Their weakness is that a tree can keep splitting until it has
memorised the training rows. In this exercise we draw a small tree, watch a
large one overfit, and then let a grid search choose how large the tree may
grow.

::: {.callout-note}
## The plots are for looking at
The code for every plot is folded away just above it, in case you are curious,
and all of it is in the notebook linked at the top of each tab. You are not
expected to write it yourself.
:::

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "rpart.plot"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(rpart.plot)            # to draw a fitted rpart tree

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables
```

The 750 people in [`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv), with
five predictors: pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree and age. The outcome has the
levels `neg` then `pos`. We keep 80% of the people for training (600) and hold
back 20% as the test set (150). `set.seed(42)` makes the split the same every
time.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — A small tree

Fit a tree that may ask at most three questions in a row (`tree_depth = 3`).
The formula `diabetes ~ .` means "use every other column as a predictor".

```{r}
tree_spec_small <- decision_tree(tree_depth = 3) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

tree_fit_small <- tree_spec_small |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
tree_fit_small |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot(extra = 104, roundint = FALSE)
```

Each box shows the predicted class, the share of `neg` and `pos` among the
people who reach it, and their share of all training rows. The first question is
about glucose. Now take the first person in the test set:

```{r}
patient <- test[1, ]
patient
```

Follow this person down the tree by hand: at each box, go left if the answer is
yes. Which leaf do they reach, and what probability of diabetes does it give?
Then check your answer with `predict()`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
predict(tree_fit_small, new_data = ______, type = "prob")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`patient` holds one row; pass it as `new_data`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
predict(tree_fit_small, new_data = patient, type = "prob")
```

This person has glucose 194. At the first box, glucose < 151 is "no", so
they go right and reach a leaf at once. In that leaf 79% of the training people
had diabetes, and `predict()` gives the same 0.789. In fact this person does
not have diabetes: a leaf gives a probability, not a certainty.
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — A tree that nothing stops overfits

rpart keeps a split only if it improves the fit by at least 1%. Switch that
rule off (`cost_complexity = 0`) and let any node with 2 or more people be split
(`min_n = 2`). Now nothing stops the tree.

```{r}
tree_spec_full <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0, min_n = 2) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

tree_fit_full <- tree_spec_full |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

tree_frame <- extract_fit_engine(tree_fit_full)$frame   # one row per node
sum(tree_frame$var == "<leaf>")                         # number of leaves
```

142 leaves for 600 people: far too many to draw. We judge it with two numbers:
accuracy, and the **AUC**. The AUC is the chance that a random person with
diabetes gets a higher predicted probability than a random person without: 0.5
is guessing, 1 is perfect. `event_level = "second"` says that `pos` is the
event. Add the predicted probabilities and classes to the training rows and to the
test rows, as in Day 4, and score both:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
tree_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc)

train_preds <- train |>
  bind_cols(predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = train, type = "prob"),
            predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = train))
tree_metrics(train_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_pos,
             event_level = "second")

test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = ______, type = "prob"),
            predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = ______))
tree_metrics(test_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_pos,
             event_level = "second")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Only the data changes: the test rows are in `test`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
tree_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc)

train_preds <- train |>
  bind_cols(predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = train, type = "prob"),
            predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = train))
tree_metrics(train_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_pos,
             event_level = "second")

test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(tree_fit_full, new_data = test))
tree_metrics(test_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_pos,
             event_level = "second")
```

The tree is perfect on the rows it was fitted on. On the test rows accuracy
falls from 1.000 to 0.607 and the AUC from 1.000 to 0.582, not much better
than guessing.
:::
:::

**Question!** What has the tree learnt from the training rows that does not
carry over to new people?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — Choosing the tree size with a grid search

How far a tree may grow is set by **hyperparameters**, like the penalty in
Exercise 5.2:

- `tree_depth`: the most questions from the top of the tree to a leaf;
- `min_n`: the fewest people a node must hold before it may be split.

We keep `cost_complexity = 0`, so that only these two restrain the tree. Mark
them with `tune()` and make a grid: five depths times five node sizes, 25
combinations.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where to find a model's hyperparameters
The help page for each model and engine lists its hyperparameters. For this
tree see
[decision trees with rpart](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/reference/details_decision_tree_rpart.html)
(or `?decision_tree`); for any other model, use the
[tidymodels model search](https://www.tidymodels.org/find/parsnip/).
:::

```{r}
tree_spec_tune <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = 0,
                                tree_depth = tune(), min_n = tune()) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

tree_grid <- grid_regular(tree_depth(range = c(1L, 10L)),
                          min_n(range = c(2L, 30L)),
                          levels = 5)
```

In Exercise 5.2 each candidate was scored on one validation set. Here we use
**5-fold cross-validation**: the training rows are cut into 5 parts (folds).
Each combination is fitted on four folds and scored on the fifth, five times
over, so that every training row is used once for scoring. The five scores are
averaged. `vfold_cv()` makes the folds; `strata = diabetes` keeps the share of
people with diabetes the same in every fold.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = diabetes)

tree_res <- tune_grid(
  tree_spec_tune,
  diabetes ~ .,
  resamples = folds,
  grid      = tree_grid,
  metrics   = metric_set(roc_auc),
  control   = control_grid(event_level = "second")
)

show_best(tree_res, metric = "roc_auc", n = 5)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
autoplot(tree_res)
```

A single question (depth 1) is too simple. When small nodes may be split
(`min_n` 2 or 9), deep trees overfit and the AUC falls. Keep the best
combination: `finalize_model()` puts it into the model, and `fit()` refits it on
all 600 training rows.

```{r}
best_tree <- select_best(tree_res, metric = "roc_auc")
best_tree

final_tree_fit <- finalize_model(tree_spec_tune, best_tree) |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)
```

Now, and only now, use the test rows. Score the chosen tree once, next to its
score on the training rows.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
final_train_preds <- train |>
  bind_cols(predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = train, type = "prob"),
            predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = train))
tree_metrics(final_train_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_pos,
             event_level = "second")

final_test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = ______, type = "prob"),
            predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = ______))
tree_metrics(final_test_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class, ______,
             event_level = "second")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The same code as in Part 2: the test rows, and the column of predicted
probabilities for `pos`, `.pred_pos`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
final_train_preds <- train |>
  bind_cols(predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = train, type = "prob"),
            predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = train))
tree_metrics(final_train_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_pos,
             event_level = "second")

final_test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = test))
tree_metrics(final_test_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_pos,
             event_level = "second")
```

The search chose `tree_depth` 7 and `min_n` 30 (cross-validated AUC 0.792).
On the test rows it has accuracy 0.700 and AUC 0.743, against 0.607 and 0.582
for the tree that nothing stopped. On the training rows it has accuracy 0.810
and AUC 0.856: the gap between training and test is much smaller.
:::
:::

**Question!** Why must the test rows play no part in choosing `tree_depth` and
`min_n`?

::: {.callout-important}
## Key points
- A tree asks one yes-or-no question at a time; each leaf gives a predicted class and a probability.
- A tree that nothing stops is perfect on its training rows and much worse on the test rows: it overfits.
- Tree depth and minimum node size are hyperparameters. Choose them with a grid search scored by cross-validation on the training rows.
- Fit the chosen tree on all the training rows, then check it once on the test rows.
:::

### Packages and data

```{python}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas matplotlib scikit-learn

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, roc_auc_score
```

The 750 people in [`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv), with
five predictors: pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree and age. The outcome is 1
for `pos` and 0 for `neg`. We keep 80% of the people for training (600) and
hold back 20% as the test set (150). `random_state=42` makes the split the same
every time.

```{python}
diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"]]
diabetes["diabetes"] = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)       # 1 = pos, 0 = neg

train, test = train_test_split(diabetes, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

predictors = ["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age"]
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — A small tree

Fit a tree that may ask at most three questions in a row (`max_depth=3`).
`random_state` fixes how ties between equally good splits are broken.

```{python}
tree_small = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=123)
tree_small = tree_small.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(16, 7))
drawn = plot_tree(tree_small, feature_names=predictors, class_names=["neg", "pos"],
                  filled=True, proportion=True, impurity=False, fontsize=9, ax=ax)
plt.show()
```

Each box shows the question, the share of training rows that reach it
(`samples`), the share of `neg` and `pos` among them (`value`) and the
predicted class. The first question is about glucose. Now take the first person
in the test set:

```{python}
patient = test.iloc[[0]]
patient
```

Follow this person down the tree by hand: at each box, go left if the answer is
true. Which leaf do they reach, and what probability of diabetes does it give?
Then check your answer with `predict_proba()`.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
tree_small.predict_proba(______[predictors])
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`patient` holds one row; pass its predictor columns.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
tree_small.predict_proba(patient[predictors])
```

This person has glucose 115, age 35 and pedigree 0.368. The answer is "true"
three times (glucose <= 154.5, age <= 36.5, pedigree <= 0.88), so they go left
three times. That leaf holds 307 training people, 14.3% of them with diabetes,
and `predict_proba()` gives the same 0.143 for `pos`.
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — A tree that nothing stops overfits

With its default settings, `DecisionTreeClassifier()` keeps splitting until
every leaf holds only one class. Nothing stops the tree.

```{python}
tree_full = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=123)
tree_full = tree_full.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

print("leaves:", tree_full.get_n_leaves())
```

135 leaves for 600 people: far too many to draw. We judge it with two numbers:
accuracy, and the **AUC**. The AUC is the chance that a random person with
diabetes gets a higher predicted probability than a random person without: 0.5
is guessing, 1 is perfect. Score the tree on the training rows and on the
test rows:

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
for name, data in [("train", train), ("test", ______)]:
    prob  = tree_full.predict_proba(data[predictors])[:, 1]   # probability of pos
    label = tree_full.predict(data[predictors])               # class, threshold 0.5
    print(name,
          "accuracy", round(accuracy_score(data["diabetes"], label), 3),
          "AUC", round(roc_auc_score(data["diabetes"], prob), 3))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Only the data changes: the test rows are in `test`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
for name, data in [("train", train), ("test", test)]:
    prob  = tree_full.predict_proba(data[predictors])[:, 1]   # probability of pos
    label = tree_full.predict(data[predictors])               # class, threshold 0.5
    print(name,
          "accuracy", round(accuracy_score(data["diabetes"], label), 3),
          "AUC", round(roc_auc_score(data["diabetes"], prob), 3))
```

The tree is perfect on the rows it was fitted on. On the test rows accuracy
falls from 1.000 to 0.673 and the AUC from 1.000 to 0.618, not much better
than guessing.
:::
:::

**Question!** What has the tree learnt from the training rows that does not
carry over to new people?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — Choosing the tree size with a grid search

How far a tree may grow is set by **hyperparameters**, like the penalty in
Exercise 5.2:

- `max_depth`: the most questions from the top of the tree to a leaf;
- `min_samples_split`: the fewest people a node must hold before it may be
  split.

In Exercise 5.2 each candidate was scored on one validation set. Here we use
**5-fold cross-validation**: the training rows are cut into 5 parts (folds).
Each combination is fitted on four folds and scored on the fifth, five times
over, so that every training row is used once for scoring. The five scores are
averaged. `cv=5` makes the folds and keeps the share of people with diabetes
the same in every fold; `scoring="roc_auc"` scores each combination by its AUC. The grid has five
depths times five node sizes, 25 combinations.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where to find a model's hyperparameters
Each scikit-learn model's page lists all its settings. For this tree see
[`DecisionTreeClassifier`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier.html);
for any other model, start from the
[API reference](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/api/index.html).
:::

```{python}
tree_grid = {"max_depth":         [1, 3, 5, 7, 10],
             "min_samples_split": [2, 9, 16, 23, 30]}

tree_search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=123),
                           param_grid=tree_grid, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
tree_search = tree_search.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

print(tree_search.best_params_)
print("cross-validated AUC:", round(tree_search.best_score_, 3))
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
tree_results = pd.DataFrame(tree_search.cv_results_)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for split in tree_grid["min_samples_split"]:
    rows = tree_results[tree_results["param_min_samples_split"] == split]
    ax.plot(rows["param_max_depth"], rows["mean_test_score"], marker="o", label=str(split))
ax.set_xlabel("max_depth")
ax.set_ylabel("Mean cross-validated AUC")
ax.legend(title="min_samples_split")
plt.show()
```

A single question (depth 1) is too simple. When small nodes may be split,
deep trees overfit and the AUC falls. `GridSearchCV()` has already refitted the
best combination on all 600 training rows:

```{python}
final_tree = tree_search.best_estimator_
```

Now, and only now, use the test rows. Score the chosen tree once, next to its
score on the training rows.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
for name, data in [("train", train), ("test", ______)]:
    prob  = final_tree.predict_proba(data[predictors])[:, 1]
    label = final_tree.predict(data[predictors])
    print(name,
          "accuracy", round(accuracy_score(data["diabetes"], label), 3),
          "AUC", round(roc_auc_score(data["diabetes"], ______), 3))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The test rows are in `test`; the AUC needs the predicted probabilities, `prob`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
for name, data in [("train", train), ("test", test)]:
    prob  = final_tree.predict_proba(data[predictors])[:, 1]
    label = final_tree.predict(data[predictors])
    print(name,
          "accuracy", round(accuracy_score(data["diabetes"], label), 3),
          "AUC", round(roc_auc_score(data["diabetes"], prob), 3))
```

The search chose `max_depth` 5 and `min_samples_split` 30 (cross-validated AUC
0.758). On the test rows it has accuracy 0.773 and AUC 0.787, against 0.673
and 0.618 for the tree that nothing stopped. On the training rows it has
accuracy 0.793 and AUC 0.862: the gap between training and test is much
smaller.
:::
:::

**Question!** Why must the test rows play no part in choosing `max_depth` and
`min_samples_split`?

::: {.callout-important}
## Key points
- A tree asks one yes-or-no question at a time; each leaf gives a predicted class and a probability.
- A tree that nothing stops is perfect on its training rows and much worse on the test rows: it overfits.
- Tree depth and minimum node size are hyperparameters. Choose them with a grid search scored by cross-validation on the training rows.
- Fit the chosen tree on all the training rows, then check it once on the test rows.
:::

::::::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Teaching choice.** Three key messages only: read a small tree, see an
unstopped tree overfit, and tune depth and node size by 5-fold cross-validation.
AUC is introduced here for the first time, in one sentence; sensitivity and
specificity (Exercise 4.3) are not repeated. R keeps `cost_complexity = 0` in
Parts 2 and 3 so that, as in Python, only depth and node size restrain the tree
(`min_n` plays the part of `min_samples_split`). The grid (depth 1 to 10,
node size 2 to 30, five levels each) is the module lead's.

**Expected values.** Split 600/150; R and Python draw different splits and
quote their own numbers. Part 1: R depth-3 tree has 4 leaves, first split
glucose < 151; first test person (glucose 194, `neg`) lands in the right-hand
leaf, P(pos) 0.789. Python depth-3 tree has 8 leaves, first split glucose
<= 154.5; first test person (glucose 115, age 35, pedigree 0.368, `neg`) goes
left three times, P(pos) 0.143. Part 2: unstopped tree R 142 leaves, Python
135; training accuracy and AUC 1.000 in both; test accuracy 0.607 (R) and
0.673 (Python), test AUC 0.582 and 0.618. Part 3 (`set.seed(123)` for the
folds in R): R best `tree_depth` 7, `min_n` 30, CV AUC 0.792 (SE 0.028);
train accuracy 0.810, AUC 0.856; test accuracy 0.700, AUC 0.743. Python best
`max_depth` 5, `min_samples_split` 30, CV AUC 0.758 (SD 0.043); train accuracy
0.793, AUC 0.862; test accuracy 0.773, AUC 0.787.

**Common failures.** (1) Calling `rpart.plot()` without `roundint = FALSE`:
it warns that it cannot retrieve the data. (2) Forgetting `event_level =
"second"`, which computes the AUC for `neg` instead of `pos`. (3) Passing the
predicted class instead of the probability to `roc_auc_score()`. (4) Tuning on
`test`. (5) Expecting a neighbour's chosen values: several combinations lie
within one standard error of the best.

**Timing.** Part 1 fifteen minutes, Part 2 fifteen, Part 3 twenty-five.
:::
:::
